evidence.claim: A swing bridge leads into a village shaped by river trade.
evidence.quote: Both landings flourished up to the American Civil War, as centers of international commerce doing business with the East and West Indies.

evidence.claim: A swing bridge leads into a village
evidence.quote: Route 82 continues east to the East Haddam Bridge over the Connecticut River, entering East Haddam near Goodspeed Opera House.

evidence.claim: Route 82 crosses the Connecticut River on the East Haddam Bridge, reaching East Haddam beside the Goodspeed Opera House.
evidence.quote: Route 82 continues east to the East Haddam Bridge over the Connecticut River, entering East Haddam near Goodspeed Opera House.

evidence.claim: The bridge itself is a designated scenic road.
evidence.quote: Route 82 is a designated scenic road for the length of the East Haddam Bridge between Haddam and East Haddam.

evidence.claim: The scenic designation continues on the first 2.31 miles of Route 149, through the historic district along the Connecticut and Moodus rivers.
evidence.quote: The section of Route 149 from the southern terminus to milepost 2.31 in East Haddam is designated as a scenic road. This portion of the road runs through the East Haddam Historic District along the banks of the Connecticut River and Moodus River.

evidence.claim: The crossing changed after a governor’s transportation commission recommended a bridge in 1909.
evidence.quote: In 1909, a Governor's commission on transportation recommended the construction of a bridge over the Connecticut River connecting East Haddam and Haddam.

evidence.claim: Connecticut redirected ferry aid toward construction, making this one of the first bridges funded by the state.
evidence.quote: the state diverted aid used to fund ferry services to building the East Haddam Bridge, becoming one of the first bridges funded by the state.

evidence.claim: Work began in April 1912; the bridge opened on June 14, 1913.
evidence.quote:
Construction of the bridge began in April 1912 and was completed in June 1913.
On June 14, 1913, Flag Day, the East Haddam Swing Bridge officially opened.

evidence.claim: The road north had another identity in the 1920s: Highway 148, renumbered Route 149 in 1932.
evidence.quote: In the 1920s, the East Haddam-Moodus-Westchester route was designated as a state highway known as Highway 148. In the 1932 state highway renumbering, old Highway 148 was renumbered to Route 149.

evidence.claim: Traveling east from Haddam, cross the three-span steel bridge into the village.
evidence.quote: The East Haddam Swing Bridge is a steel, movable (swing) truss bridge. The bridge is composed of three spans crossing the Connecticut River between Haddam, Connecticut and East Haddam, Connecticut.

evidence.claim: At Route 149, Main Street leads north beside the Connecticut, then northeast along the Moodus River as East Haddam-Moodus Road.
evidence.quote: Route 149 begins as Main Street at an intersection with Route 82 in town center of East Haddam and heads north along the Connecticut River, then northeast as East Haddam-Moodus Road along the Moodus River.

evidence.claim: The historic district follows this road in a long line: the former Upper and Lower Landings grew together where steep ground to the east limited expansion.
evidence.quote: The Upper and Lower Landings each developed somewhat independently, but over time became united into a long linear village, caused in part by the steep terrain immediately to the east which limited growth in that direction.

evidence.claim: The East Haddam crossing makes room for two kinds of traffic: Route 82 above and river travel through its movable span.
evidence.quote: The bridge carries Route 82

evidence.claim: Alfred P. Boller designed the drawbridge to pivot, clearing a passage for vessels.
evidence.quote: The pin-connected drawbridge was designed by Alfred P. Boller, an authority on deep bridge foundations, to allow the bridge to pivot/swing, clearing a path for through river travel.

evidence.claim: Its three spans total 889 feet, including a 461-foot swing span.
evidence.quote: and a swing span (461 ft long). Together they bring the total length of the swing bridge to 889 ft.

evidence.claim: The opening on Flag Day in 1913 brought a speech by Governor Simeon E. Baldwin, a 17-gun salute and a Model-T parade.
evidence.quote: On June 14, 1913, Flag Day, the East Haddam Swing Bridge officially opened. It was hailed as an ornament to the "age of progressiveness". The celebration included an address by Governor Simeon E. Baldwin, a 17-gun salute, a Model-T automobile parade

evidence.claim: Below the riveted steel, stone-block piers and abutments rest on timber pilings.
evidence.quote: The stone-block piers and abutments are built on timber pilings.

evidence.claim: Three steel spans cross the river; the swing span is 461 feet long.
evidence.quote: The 3 spans of the bridge are all composed of rivet-connecting steel members. From west to east, the three spans include: A Warren deck truss (101 ft long), a Pennsylvania through truss (327 ft long and one of the longest in the state), and a swing span (461 ft long).

evidence.claim: The theater at Goodspeed occupies the building’s top two floors.
evidence.quote: The theater itself is actually located on the top two floors of the building

evidence.claim: Scenery travels up from the dock area through a vacant shaft equipped with a winch.
evidence.quote: Scenery is loaded in from the dock area up a vacant shaft outfitted with a winch system to haul the scenery up to the stage level.

evidence.claim: Merchant and banker William Henry Goodspeed built the venue in 1876–1877 for plays, despite its operatic name.
evidence.quote: The Opera House was originally built by a local merchant and banker, William Henry Goodspeed. Construction began in 1876 and finished in 1877. Despite the name, it was not in fact an opera house, but rather a venue for presenting plays.

evidence.claim: After his death, its uses included a militia base, general store and transportation department storage.
evidence.quote: After William Goodspeed's death in 1882, the opera house fell into disrepair, facing a series of less glamorous uses—from a militia base during World War I to a general store and a Department of Transportation storage facility.

evidence.claim: In 1959, citizens formed Goodspeed Musicals after the state condemned the building.
evidence.quote: Goodspeed Musicals was formed in 1959 by a group of concerned citizens after the state of Connecticut had condemned the building.

evidence.claim: Restoration led to its rededication in 1963.
evidence.quote: The restoration project took nearly four years, and the Goodspeed Opera House was rededicated on June 8, 1963.

evidence.claim: Upper Landing and Lower Landing once traded with the East and West Indies.
evidence.quote: Both landings flourished up to the American Civil War, as centers of international commerce doing business with the East and West Indies.

evidence.claim: After the Civil War, their commercial importance declined as rail transport rose on the river’s west bank.
evidence.quote: The landings declined in economic importance after the war, owing to the rise of the railroad as the principal means of commercial transport, which was run up the west side of the river.

evidence.claim: The southern landing developed as a tourist destination and contains the bridge and village commercial district.
evidence.quote: The southern landing eventually became more significant as a tourist destination, and is where the East Haddam Bridge is now located, as is the village's commercial district.

evidence.claim: Its cemetery, park and monuments to Nathan Hale and General Joseph Spencer add other layers to the riverside village.
evidence.quote: Also included in the district are two monuments, one to Nathan Hale and another to Gen. Joseph Spencer, a park, and a cemetery.

evidence.claim: The bridge combines a deck truss, a through truss and a swing span, with steel members joined by rivets.
evidence.quote: The 3 spans of the bridge are all composed of rivet-connecting steel members. From west to east, the three spans include: A Warren deck truss (101 ft long), a Pennsylvania through truss (327 ft long and one of the longest in the state), and a swing span (461 ft long).

evidence.claim: The river landings had already lost commercial importance after the Civil War, when the railroad on the opposite bank became the principal freight connection.
evidence.quote: The landings declined in economic importance after the war, owing to the rise of the railroad as the principal means of commercial transport, which was run up the west side of the river.

evidence.claim: Special commissions oversaw construction because the State Highway Department then lacked authority over bridges.
evidence.quote: At the time, the State Highway Department had no authority over bridges. This meant the state legislature formed special commissions took the lead on building the East Haddam Bridge.

evidence.claim: The state agreed to sell it to the group for one dollar, on condition that they raise enough to restore and maintain it.
evidence.quote: The state agreed to sell the building to the group for one dollar, provided they acquire enough funding to restore and maintain it.

evidence.claim: The district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1983

evidence.claim: The 110-acre historic district
evidence.quote: The East Haddam Historic District is a 110-acre (45 ha) historic district in East Haddam, Connecticut.

evidence.claim: gathers buildings from both settlements along Route 149
evidence.quote: It includes buildings from two 18th-century settlements of the town on the east bank of the Connecticut River, Upper Landing and Lower Landing. The district is linear and runs along Route 149.

evidence.claim: including the town’s principal civic structures and Goodspeed Opera House
evidence.quote: as well as the town's main civic structures, and the Goodspeed Opera House.

flags: Cache establishes scenic-road limits but contains no designation-body explanation, drive time, grades or curves; no such details added.
Ferry start dates disagree: bridge history gives 1694, district history 1695. Omitted the precise date.
Material supplies only Johnsonville as a strip town; retained landmarks ordered west-to-east across the bridge, then north along Route 149 using cached route descriptions.
No current claims were dropped for lack of cache support. The attributed Annie scenery anecdote was omitted to focus on building reuse.
